newsitem.title: USA: Clinton satisfied with White House-FBI relations.
newsitem.headline: Clinton satisfied with White House-FBI relations.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Wednesday he believed he and the FBI had a good working relationship despite two recent cases in which the law enforcement agency apparently kept information from him.
Clinton, speaking with reporters at the start of a meeting with Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic, also gave FBI director Louis Freeh a qualified vote of confidence.
"I don't have any information at this time which would call into question that confidence," he said.

The president was responding to questions about a New York Times report on Tuesday that the Federal Bureau of Investigation had denied a White House request for information about alleged Chinese efforts to meddle in U.S. politics.

It was the second such incident to come to light in recent weeks. The first, ultimately blamed on a misunderstanding, was an FBI warning in 1996 about alleged Chinese interference in U.S. politics that two National Security Council aides believed they were not supposed to pass on to their superiors.

Quoting U.S. officials, the newspaper said Freeh rebuffed a request by White House Counsel Charles Ruff last month for material to brief Secretary of State Madeleine Albright before she visited Beijing. According to the report, some information was provided to the White House after Freeh consulted with Attorney General Janet Reno.

While conceding that "you don't know what you don't get," Clinton said he had "no evidence on which I can say we have not been able to get the information we need." He said the FBI had a "dual obligation" to provide administration policymakers with the information they need to protect and advance U.S. national security and at the same time to preserve the integrity of criminal investigations.

Alleged Chinese efforts to buy U.S. political influence by funneling cash into last year's presidential and congressional election campaigns -- which, if true, would be illegal -- are now the subject of several probes. China strongly denied the allegations again this week during Vice President Al Gore's meeting with Chinese Prime Minister Li Peng in Beijing.
Clinton said it was up to Reno to resolve conflicts in information-sharing and that "ultimately those things almost have to be resolved on a case-by-case basis."

Clinton's Democratic Party has returned nearly $3 million to campaign contributors -- most of them individuals with ties to Asian business interests or governments -- that were deemed questionable or improper. At least a dozen committees of the Republican-led Congress are looking into different aspects of the campaign financing controversy.

Sensitivity about White House dealings with the FBI dates back to the early months of Clinton's presidency when White House officials improperly involved the law enforcement agency in a purge of the White House travel office in 1993.
